clinicalPearls: SPG18 is caused by variants in ERLIN2; it is most often autosomal recessive, though dominant families with a milder, sometimes pure phenotype have been reported.
The recessive form is a complicated HSP of early childhood, combining spastic paraplegia with intellectual disability and joint contractures.
Seizures may occur, adding to the complicated picture and distinguishing it from pure autosomal HSP.
ERLIN2 is allelic with a juvenile motor neuron disorder, so some patients present within a juvenile primary lateral sclerosis or juvenile amyotrophic lateral sclerosis spectrum.
Its sibling gene ERLIN1 causes SPG62, and the two proteins act together, so the phenotypes overlap conceptually.
Brain imaging may reveal a thin corpus callosum and non-specific white-matter changes in some individuals.
Early contractures and cognitive impairment in a child with lower-limb spasticity should raise suspicion of an autosomal recessive complicated HSP such as this one.
Consanguinity or affected siblings with unaffected parents supports the recessive inheritance pattern.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG18 is caused by variants in ERLIN2, which encodes endoplasmic reticulum lipid raft-associated protein 2, a member of the SPFH (stomatin/prohibitin/flotillin/HflK-C) domain family. ERLIN2 assembles with ERLIN1 into a large oligomeric complex embedded in endoplasmic reticulum membrane lipid rafts. This complex is a key regulator of endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation, most notably mediating the ubiquitin-dependent turnover of activated inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptors, and it also participates in cholesterol and lipid homeostasis and in handling of misfolded membrane proteins. Loss of ERLIN2 function perturbs intracellular calcium signalling and lipid raft integrity within neurons, and long corticospinal motor axons appear particularly vulnerable, producing the spastic paraparesis; more severe disruption manifests within the juvenile motor neuron disease end of the spectrum.

additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain and spinal cord, assessing the corpus callosum and white matter
Molecular analysis of ERLIN2, typically within an HSP gene panel
Electromyography and nerve conduction studies to evaluate motor neuron involvement
Assessment of contractures with input from rehabilitation and orthopaedics
redFlags: Emergence of bulbar signs (dysarthria, dysphagia) suggesting a juvenile motor neuron disease overlap
Respiratory muscle involvement or declining respiratory function
Rapid motor deterioration outpacing the usual slow HSP course
reference.prognosis: The recessive complicated form usually presents in early childhood and progresses slowly, with disability driven by spasticity, contractures and cognitive impairment; individuals within the juvenile motor neuron disease overlap have a less favourable course.
pitfalls: Confusing SPG18 with SPG11 or SPG15 because all share a thin corpus callosum and cognitive involvement
Failing to recognise the juvenile primary lateral sclerosis/amyotrophic lateral sclerosis overlap when motor decline is prominent
Missing autosomal recessive inheritance in small or non-consanguineous families
Overlooking the related ERLIN1 (SPG62) disorder in the differential
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: No disease-specific therapy exists; treat spasticity with oral antispasticity agents and focal botulinum toxin, with intrathecal baclofen reserved for severe cases
Intensive physiotherapy, serial stretching, orthoses and orthopaedic input to prevent and treat the characteristic joint contractures
Antiseizure medication for the epilepsy seen in the complicated recessive form
Developmental, educational and neuropsychological support for intellectual disability
Monitor for the juvenile motor-neuron-disease overlap, with respiratory and nutritional surveillance if bulbar or motor decline emerges
Genetic counselling with cascade ERLIN2 testing for autosomal recessive inheritance
Escalate to multidisciplinary paediatric neurology for contracture surgery or difficult seizure control
